newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Taleban breach enemy defences in key pass.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban breach enemy defences in key pass.

text.p: Afghanistan's Islamic Taleban militia burst through opposition defences to capture three key towns and part of the Salang Pass north of Kabul in a dawn assault on Thursday, witnesses said.

The Taleban warriors, who seized the Soviet-built Bagram airbase and town of Charikar a week ago, thrust north to take the towns of Jabal-os-Siraj, Gulbahar and Ghorband, dealing a devastating blow to three loosely allied opposition factions.

They then pushed up the Salang Pass to within 20 km (13 miles) of the Soviet-built tunnel that leads over the formidable Hindu Kush mountain range into northern provinces held by Uzbek opposition general Abdul Rashid Dostum.

The fall of Gulbahar, 15 km (nine miles) northeast of the garrison town of Jabal-os-Siraj, means the Taleban once again threaten the Panjsher Valley, bastion of ousted government military commander Ahmad Shah Masood.
Ghorband, 30 km (19 miles) west of Jabal-os-Siraj, had been a stronghold of ethnic Hazaras, Shi'ite Moslems who support the Hizb-i-Wahdat group within the anti-Taleban alliance.

"The attack on Jabal-os-Siraj started from the main road of Charikar and from Kapisa province early in the morning," Taleban acting Information Minister Amir Khan Mutaqi told reporters at the town at the foot of the Salang Pass. "Our forces have captured more than 200 prisoners and more than 40 tanks."

But a Taleban spokesman at the movement's headquarters in the southern city of Kandahar, quoted by a Pakistan-based private Afghan news service, later said the militia had captured more than 500 opposition fighters.
The Afghan Islamic Press quoted the spokesman as saying that Masood and his forces had fled to Panjsher and blocked the road leading to it by dynamiting a moutainside.
Some of the few residents left in Jabal-os-Siraj said the semi-deserted town had fallen with little resistance, apparently due to disputes between rival commanders of Dostum's in the area.
Taleban fighters were moving systematically from house to house in search of guns and opposition fighters. Most civilians fled the town after last week's advances by the Taleban.

Further north, Taleban fighters had put 18 of captured Uzbek soldiers on display on a muddy verge of the road winding up the Salang Pass. The prisoners sat crosslegged with their hands tied behind their backs, one with a bleeding wound in his leg.
Taleban forces were hunting down fleeing Dostum fighters on the mountainsides, shooting at any who did not surrender, as sporadic artillery fire echoed through the narrow pass.

The sudden appearance of one of Dostum's fighter jets prompted deafening bursts of anti-aircraft fire. Witnesses in Jabal-os-Siraj said a Dostum plane had bombed the town, but there were no immediate reports of casualties.
Jalaluddin Haqqani, a senior Taleban commander, told a U.N. diplomat who visited the Salang Pass that the Islamic movement would not offer any truce to what he called "mercenaries".
"We will continue our operation until Masood and Dostum are finished," Haqqani told Stephen Evans, a political adviser to the U.N. special envoy to Afghanistan, Norbert Holl.
Haqqani accused the opposition leaders of being backed by Iran and Russia, saying formation of a coalition government of all factions was not the way to solve the Afghan conflict.
The only option for Masood and Dostum was to surrender or flee the country, Haqqani declared.
Taleban forces are now back where they were soon after driving Masood's forces and the Tajik-dominated government led by Burhanuddin Rabbani out of Kabul on September 27.
At that time Masood retreated inside the Panjsher Valley, dynamiting the steep hillsides at its mouth to create landslides that prevented the Taleban from moving armour inside.
